records.title: perf: relational-program — 426→17.6 ms littleX feed, phased breakdown and branch map
records.body:
## Goal

Close the gap between Jac's Postgres-native runtime and the measured **SQLAlchemy ORM bar (server p50 30.2 ms)** on the littleX feed workload (2,552-item feed, 100 profiles, 5k tweets, 5k follows). Hand-tuned PG baseline (14 ms) acknowledged as out of scope — residual is per-row runtime semantics, not schema.

**Result: 426 ms → 17.6 ms (~24×), under the ORM bar.** Every step ships with value-parity vs `JAC_STREAM=0`, the 58-test suite, and the DB write oracle.

Full history on `perf/relational-program` (tip `d87b98bf1`, base `ea5f764ad`). The work is split into four stacked phase branches — each is a runnable snapshot of the cumulative state at that phase's end, and the diff between consecutive branches isolates exactly one phase's contribution:

| phase branch | tip | contribution | feed p50 at tip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `perf/phase1-micro-opts` | `ce219b2e2` | runtime micro-opts | ~178 ms |
| `perf/phase2-zero-materialization` | `eb000b032` | compiler-proven streaming | ~96 ms |
| `perf/phase3-relational-mirrors` | `8b85f2b92` | relational program R1–R4 | ~28.7 ms |
| `perf/phase4-topk-pushdown` | `d87b98bf1` | distributed top-K pushdown | ~17.6 ms |

## Phase 1 — runtime micro-opts (426 → 178 ms)

Profiling-driven fixes on the serialize/deserialize and DB round-trip paths:

- typed emit-plan serializer (no per-object `dir()` scan), orjson, report-echo gate (`d7bbf53d6`)
- dirty-bit tracking: flush O(mutated) not O(resident) (`d7bbf53d6`, ctx fix in phase 2)
- typed-endpoint edge index (`src_type`/`dst_type` denormalised, NULL-tolerant) + batched ACL root prefetch: 62 → 12 stmts/request (`21b7f2252`)
- fingerprint-trusted deserialize + server GC freeze (p95 533 → 283) (`2097b27f3`)
- C-level bulk dict fill (`a8f761197`), (id, xmin)-keyed response-fragment memo (`96970b63c`)
- drop the 110 ms/request hash re-serialisation (`aa757b1f4`), interned str→UUID (`ce219b2e2`)

Instructive failures kept in history: lazy adjacency reverted for overlay/cascade semantics (`8ec6f1a7b`/`982c53beb`); hash-sentinel permission bypass caught by tests (`a7788ac19`).

## Phase 2 — compiler-proven zero-materialization (178 → 96 ms)

- **StreamProofPass** (`c4b7e1862`): new compiler pass audits every use of every chain-expression result in a walker; if all observations are trivial (list plumbing, `len`/subscript, `jid()`, scalar field reads, single-field sort keys, final `report`), stamps `__jac_stream_fields__`. Flow-insensitive ⇒ can only over-taint ⇒ over-approval impossible.
- **StreamNode**: proof-gated stand-in serving field reads from stored props — no archetype, Permission, or edge-stub construction. `__setattr__` raises loudly.
- Consumption-aware membership pushdown: `x in [chain]` → `chain_has(x, query)`; follow_user write 37 → 4.3 ms (`310ae86d3`)
- fix: dirty-marking targeted the wrong execution context on the served path — writes silently dropped at flush, caught by the write oracle (`6f63b6921`)
- design docs record the measured verdict: relational rewrite worth 1.4×, not 7× (`a7ca9ee88`, `eb000b032`)

## Phase 3 — relational program R1–R4 (96 → 28.7 ms)

GO decision (`2323d3566`): target the ORM bar with derived state, not a schema rewrite.

- **R1/R2/R4** (`a5c3aac34`): per-node-archetype mirror tables (`g_n_<type>_<mod6>`) maintained by triggers on `anchors` in the same txn — anchors stays source of truth, mirrors rebuildable, write path untouched (~0.3 ms trigger cost). Rows carry typed field columns, the **prebuilt API response fragment as text** (fed verbatim to `orjson.Fragment`; Python never parses props), and ACL scalars enabling an exact-semantics fast path. 96 → 41.9 ms.
- **R3** (`8b85f2b92`): fused single-statement stream query — final hop joins the mirror (membership is the type test), returning fragment/ACL/proof columns directly. One statement replaces traversal + fetch. 40.1 → **28.7 ms, under the SQLAlchemy bar**.

## Phase 4 — distributed top-K pushdown (29.7 → 17.6 ms)

`d87b98bf1`: StreamProofPass recognises the sort-then-slice pipeline idiom (one single-field sort + one constant-bound report slice), emits `__jac_stream_pipeline__ = (field, desc, K)`. The fused query fetches only top-(K+slack) per chain source ordered by the mirror's typed column; top-K containment makes the merged result value-identical. Runtime re-guards trigger an unlimited rerun on any violation. Top-20 page: 29.7 → 17.6 ms.

## Design invariant

Every optimization follows: **prove statically, re-guard dynamically, fall back to slow-correct.** Analysis bugs degrade to the materialized path, never to wrong answers. Parity vs `JAC_STREAM=0` maintained at every commit.

## References

- `jac/docs/design/typed-relational-backend.md` — measured gap decomposition + GO decision
- `jac/docs/design/stream-proof-plan.md` — proof contract + kill conditions
- `jac/docs/design/relational-r1r4-implementation.md` — mirror design + shipped status

## Open items

- R3 full commitment: per-edge-type tables + id directory + untyped

records.title: Daily Perf Improver: Research and Plan
records.body:
# Daily Perf Improver: Research and Plan

## Overview
This issue documents the performance improvement research and planning for the Tokio runtime. The goal is to systematically identify, measure, and optimize performance bottlenecks in the Tokio ecosystem.

## Performance Testing Infrastructure

### Benchmarking Setup
- **Tool**: Criterion.rs for micro-benchmarks
- **Location**: `benches/` directory with 15 benchmark categories
- **Commands**: 
  - `cd benches && cargo bench` - Run all benchmarks
  - `cargo bench --bench [specific]` - Run specific benchmark
  - `cargo bench [function_name]` - Run specific benchmark function

### Key Benchmark Categories
1. **spawn** - Task spawning performance (current_thread vs multi_thread)
2. **sync_broadcast** - Broadcast channel performance  
3. **sync_mpsc** - Multi-producer single-consumer channels
4. **sync_mpsc_oneshot** - Oneshot channel performance
5. **sync_watch** - Watch channel performance
6. **sync_notify** - Notification primitive performance
7. **sync_rwlock** - Read-write lock performance
8. **sync_semaphore** - Semaphore performance
9. **rt_current_thread** - Single-threaded runtime performance
10. **rt_multi_threaded** - Multi-threaded runtime performance
11. **fs** - Filesystem operation performance
12. **copy** - I/O copy operation performance
13. **time_now** - Time-related operations
14. **time_timeout** - Timeout operations
15. **signal** - Signal handling performance

## Critical Performance Areas Identified

### 1. Work-Stealing Task Scheduler
**Location**: `tokio/src/runtime/scheduler/multi_thread/`

**Key Components**:
- **Queue System** (`queue.rs`): Local task queues with 256-task capacity
- **Worker Threads** (`worker.rs`): Work-stealing algorithm implementation
- **Task Distribution**: Load balancing across worker threads

**Potential Optimizations**:
- Queue size tuning (current: 256 tasks per worker)
- Steal batch size optimization
- Memory layout improvements for cache locality
- Atomic operation optimization (ABA problem mitigation)

### 2. Task Spawning Performance
**Current Benchmarks**: Basic scheduler vs threaded scheduler spawn performance

**Areas for Improvement**:
- Task allocation and deallocation optimization
- Spawn latency reduction
- Batch spawning optimizations
- Memory pool improvements for task storage

### 3. Synchronization Primitives
**Critical for Application Performance**:
- **Broadcast channels**: Fan-out message distribution
- **MPSC channels**: Producer-consumer communication
- **RwLock**: Concurrent read/write access patterns
- **Semaphore**: Resource limiting performance
- **Notify**: Task coordination primitive

### 4. I/O System Performance
**Location**: `tokio/src/runtime/io/`

**Key Areas**:
- Event registration and polling efficiency
- ScheduledIo waker management
- Cross-platform I/O driver optimization
- Socket and file I/O performance

### 5. Time and Timer System
**Areas**: Time wheel implementation, timeout handling, sleep/interval performance

## Performance Goals by Round

### Round 1 (Low-hanging fruit - 2-4 weeks)
- [ ] **Task spawn optimization**: Improve single task spawn latency by 5-10%
- [ ] **Work-stealing tuning**: Optimize steal batch sizes and queue parameters
- [ ] **Benchmark expansion**: Add micro-benchmarks for missing scenarios
- [ ] **Memory allocation analysis**: Profile and optimize task/waker allocations

### Round 2 (Algorithm improvements - 1-2 months)  
- [ ] **Scheduler enhancements**: Implement cache-aware work stealing
- [ ] **Lock-free optimizations**: Reduce contention in sync primitives
- [ ] **I/O batching**: Optimize I/O event processing batches
- [ ] **Timer wheel improvements**: Optimize time wheel data structure

### Round 3 (Advanced optimizations - 2-3 months)
- [ ] **NUMA awareness**: Scheduler improvements for multi-socket systems
- [ ] **Vectorization**: SIMD optimizations where applicable  
- [ ] **Platform-specific optimizations**: io_uring, kqueue, IOCP improvements
- [ ] **Profile-guided optimization**: Use PGO for hot path optimization

## Development Workflow

### Performance Measurement Commands
```bash
# Build with optimizations
cargo build --release --all-features

# Run specific benchmarks
cd benches
cargo bench --bench spawn
cargo bench --bench rt_multi_threaded  
cargo bench --bench sync_mpsc

# Profile with perf (Linux)
cargo build --release --all-features
perf record --call-graph=lbr cargo bench --bench [target]
perf report

# Memory profiling with valgrind
cargo build --all-features
valgrind --tool=cachegrind cargo bench --bench [target]
```

### Testing Commands  
```bash
# Full test suite
cargo test --all-features

# Loom concurrency testing
cd tokio
LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS=1 LOOM_MAX_BRANCHES=10000 RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom -C debug_assertions" \
    cargo test --lib --release --features full -- --test-threads=1

# Miri testing
MIRIFLAGS="-Zmiri-disable-isolation -Zmiri-strict-provenance -Zmiri-retag-fields" \
    cargo +nightly miri test --features

records.title: FINAL ARCHITECTURE AUDIT — 100% codebase modernization and AI-central evolution
Harden Carve lineage and graph decisions
records.body:
## Parent

#37

## What to build

Harden the completed Carve path for regeneration, difficult migration shapes, graph defects, collisions, and unresolved planning pressure. The planner must preserve traceability, keep semantic dependencies minimal, and stop with a needs-decision result instead of publishing a plan that invents requirements or hides an invalid graph.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Regenerating an unchanged proposal preserves candidate identities. Splits and combinations create explicit replacement lineage without reusing an identity for changed work.
- [ ] A true shared prerequisite can be represented as a prefactor ticket only when later tickets consume its concrete output; the planner does not create a shared convenience foundation.
- [ ] Expand-contract work records expansion, independently mergeable migration groups, and contraction in dependency order. Contraction depends directly on every migration group that must complete first, and plans that cannot keep each group green record the required integration point.
- [ ] Migration strategy remains separate from ticket shape for normal, prefactor, and expand-contract plans.
- [ ] Collisions are recorded as non-blocking metadata. They do not create semantic dependency edges or remove unrelated tickets from the calculated frontier.
- [ ] Plan validation rejects missing dependency targets, cycles, redundant transitive blockers, convenience foundations, skeletal tickets, and uncovered requirements before publication.
- [ ] Unsettled requirements, unresolved Ticket Scope flags, or pressure that requires a human choice produce a needs-decision plan with the unresolved choice stated. Needs-decision plans never publish tickets.
- [ ] Frontier calculation uses only valid direct dependency edges and remains stable across equivalent regenerations.
- [ ] Pressure cases cover stable lineage, split and combine replacement, prefactoring, expand-contract migration, overlapping collisions, every rejected graph defect, and needs-decision publication refusal.
- [ ] Behavioral cases observe outputs and attempted mutations rather than exact prose, internal call counts, worker topology, or private helper structure.

## Blocked by

- #40

records.title: feat: task dependencies, phases, and workflow view
records.body:
## Problem

Current task system is flat — each task is independent. No way to express:
- Task A must finish before Task B starts
- Multiple tasks belong to the same phase and run in parallel
- A workflow consists of ordered phases with fan-out/fan-in patterns
- Conditional retry (reject → redo previous phase)

## Motivating Example

Investment analysis pipeline with 6 phases, ~12 tasks:

```
Phase 1 — Data Collection (parallel)
├─ Market Analyst
├─ News Analyst
├─ Sentiment Analyst
└─ Fundamentals
    → all feed into Research Package

Phase 2 — Independent Thesis (parallel, isolated)
├─ Bull Researcher
└─ Bear Researcher
    → two independent theses

Phase 3 — Cross Debate (sequential, randomized)
Bull ⇄ Bear (N rounds)
    → Research Manager produces Investment Thesis

Phase 4 — Risk Assessment (parallel, based on thesis)
├─ Aggressive
├─ Neutral
└─ Conservative
    → Risk Manager consolidates constraints

Phase 5 — Trade Design (constrained)
Trader receives Thesis + Risk Constraints
    → designs execution plan within framework

Phase 6 — Final Decision
Portfolio Manager reviews
    → approve / reject / modify
    → reject loops back to Phase 5 (max 1 retry)
```

None of this is expressible with the current flat task list.

## Proposed Design

### Data Model Changes

Add to task schema:
- `depends_on: taskId[]` — this task is blocked until all dependencies are done
- `parent_task_id: string | null` — groups tasks into a workflow (all tasks sharing the same root parent)
- `phase: string` — display grouping label (e.g. "Phase 1 — Data Collection")

### Platform Behavior

1. Task with unmet dependencies starts in `blocked` status
2. When all `depends_on` tasks reach `done` → platform auto-transitions task to `open` and sends assignment message
3. Topological sort determines execution order
4. Circular dependency detection on creation (reject with error)

### Data Flow Between Phases

- Each task's thread content IS its output
- Downstream task's assignment preamble includes summary/links to upstream threads
- Platform provides the plumbing, agent does the synthesis

### Orchestration Pattern

1. An orchestrator task (or human) creates all tasks with dependencies in one batch
2. Platform handles the scheduling DAG
3. Orchestrator monitors overall progress, handles retries/exceptions

### UI — Workflow View in Tasks Tab

When tasks have `parent_task_id`, the Tasks tab switches from flat table to **phased workflow view**:

```
Phase 1 — Data Collection              ████████ 4/4 done ✅
  ├ #25 Market Analyst      ● Done
  ├ #26 News Analyst        ● Done
  ├ #27 Sentiment Analyst   ● Done
  └ #28 Fundamentals        ● Done

Phase 2 — Independent Thesis           ████░░░░ 1/2 in_progress
  ├ #29 Bull Researcher     ◉ In Progress
  └ #30 Bear Researcher     ○ Open

Phase 3 — Cross Debate                 ░░░░░░░░ blocked
  └ #31 Bull vs Bear        ◌ Blocked (depends on #29, #30)
```

Key elements:
- **Phase grouping** with collapsible sections + progress bar per phase
- **Dependency visualization** — blocked tasks show what they're waiting for
- **Real-time updates** via WebSocket (task status changes → progress bars update)
- **Thread integration** — click task row to open thread panel
- **Global progress** — top bar: "Phase 2 of 6 · 6/12 tasks done"
- **Flat tasks** (no parent) keep the current table view — both coexist

## Design Principles

- **Platform does scheduling** — topological sort, auto-trigger, dependency tracking
- **Agent does planning** — decides what tasks to create, what dependencies to set
- **Each does what it's good at** — platform is reliable infrastructure, agent is flexible intelligence

## Implementation Phases

1. **Schema** — add depends_on, parent_task_id, phase fields + migration
2. **Engine** — dependency resolution, auto-trigger on completion, blocked status
3. **API** — batch task creation, dependency validation
4. **UI** — workflow view with phases, progress bars, dependency indicators
5. **Orchestrator pattern** — document how agents create and manage workflows

records.title: Define and enforce the supported iOS GenAI capability boundary
records.body:
## Problem

The custom `v0.10.26` distribution builds the public CPU GenAI implementation because the upstream source tag references iOS-specific implementation files that are not published.

The compatibility layer preserves the public API surface, but `CGImage` input returns `kUnimplemented`. Without an explicit, machine-readable capability contract, consumers could assume parity with Google's complete iOS GenAI binaries or silently expose unsupported features.

## Scope

- Define supported and unsupported GenAI operations for this distribution
- Publish capability information in a stable form consumable by Eyespie
- Fail clearly for unsupported image or GPU-backed paths
- Document expected performance and device implications of CPU-only inference
- Distinguish source compatibility, ABI compatibility, and behavioral support
- Establish a removal and migration path when upstream publishes a complete implementation

## Capability contract

The contract must explicitly represent at least:

- backend: `public_cpu_only`
- text generation: supported status and tested model families
- `CGImage` input: unsupported
- GPU acceleration: unavailable/not claimed
- minimum iOS and architecture matrix
- source revision and distribution version

The metadata may be exposed through a packaged manifest, framework metadata, generated header/API, or another stable mechanism, but it must ship with or be deterministically associated with the consumed artifacts. A CI-only provenance file is insufficient for runtime feature gating unless it is propagated downstream.

## Error behavior

Unsupported APIs must:

- return a stable error code;
- provide an actionable message;
- avoid partial state mutation;
- avoid implying successful GPU or multimodal initialization;
- remain covered by ABI and behavior tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Supported text-generation operations and tested model families are documented
- [ ] Unsupported `CGImage` input returns a stable, actionable error
- [ ] No API silently falls back while implying GPU acceleration or multimodal parity
- [ ] A stable artifact-associated capability manifest exposes `public_cpu_only`
- [ ] Downstream Eyespie integration can gate features using the capability contract
- [ ] Release notes clearly distinguish this build from Google's complete binary distribution
- [ ] Source compatibility, ABI compatibility, and behavioral support are documented separately
- [ ] A migration test and removal criteria exist for replacing the compatibility backend later
- [ ] Device benchmark results from #3 are linked before production suitability is claimed

## Non-goals

- Reimplementing Google's unpublished iOS GPU backend
- Claiming that ABI-compatible stubs provide feature parity
- Encoding Eyespie-specific UI policy inside MediaPipe artifacts

## Context

- Distribution implementation: #2
- Physical-device characterization: #3
- Real consumer integration: `ryjen/eyespie#78`

Current provenance:

- `genai_backend=public_cpu_only`
- `genai_cgimage_input=unsupported`

## Upstream references

- google-ai-edge/mediapipe#6234 — public iOS GenAI build references missing `llm_inference_engine_ios` sources
- google-ai-edge/mediapipe#6167 — Apple package construction and missing linked content

records.title: ATYA-039 — Replace platform drift JavaScript with CLI fleet audits
records.body:
## Task metadata

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| ATYA ID | ATYA-039 |
| Owning repository | Atya.Roadmap |
| Priority | P1 |
| Phase | 3 — Build, workflow, and release consolidation |
| Type | Verification |
| Initial status | Blocked |
| Hard dependencies | ATYA-038; ATYA-019; ATYA-001; ATYA-124 |
| Advisory prerequisites | None |

| Origin | Merged (S-0020 + F-0035 (drift-checks half)) |
| Confidence | High |
| Risk | High |
| Effort | M |

## Problem description

Platform drift is a large inline JS implementation checking shallow structure, duplicating policy, mishandling infra repos; the standing checks this plan needs (tree parity, tag ancestry, SHA pins, matrix drift, pin currency, README sections, release traceability) don't exist as machinery.

## Root cause

Fleet policy and implementation evolved in separate repositories without one enforced source of truth or evidence gate. Platform drift is a large inline JS implementation checking shallow structure, duplicating policy, mishandling infra repos; the standing checks this plan needs (tree parity, tag ancestry, SHA pins, matrix drift, pin currency, README sections, release traceability) don't exist as machinery.

## Desired outcome

SHA-pin a released CLI in the scheduled workflow; atya doctor --fleet with manifest-driven archetypes emitting machine-readable results into the existing read-only issue flow; checks: master==development trees, newest-tag ancestry, workflow SHA == fleet pin, csproj refs == manifest edges, global.json == fleet-current, README mandatory sections, tag/Release/NuGet traceability; fixture-tested exceptions; no fleet mutation.

## Affected scope

Primary owner: **Atya.Roadmap**. Audit-affected repositories or coordination scopes: Atya.Roadmap, Cli, platform. Only the cited findings and their direct acceptance evidence are added; unaffected architecture remains unchanged.

## In-scope work

platform drift workflow; CLI. SHA-pin a released CLI in the scheduled workflow; atya doctor --fleet with manifest-driven archetypes emitting machine-readable results into the existing read-only issue flow; checks: master==development trees, newest-tag ancestry, workflow SHA == fleet pin, csproj refs == manifest edges, global.json == fleet-current, README mandatory sections, tag/Release/NuGet traceability; fixture-tested exceptions; no fleet mutation.

## Out-of-scope work

Unrelated repositories or public APIs, speculative package creation, and destructive cleanup not explicitly named by this task.

## Hard dependencies

- ATYA-038
- ATYA-019
- ATYA-001
- ATYA-124

## Advisory prerequisites

None. Advisory prerequisites are nonblocking and do not affect Ready/Blocked status.

## Related tasks

- ATYA-001
- ATYA-002
- ATYA-003

## Implementation sequence

1. Inspect the cited repository paths, public APIs, workflows, tests, tags, and open work before changing anything.
2. SHA-pin a released CLI in the scheduled workflow
3. atya doctor --fleet with manifest-driven archetypes emitting machine-readable results into the existing read-only issue flow
4. checks: master==development trees, newest-tag ancestry, workflow SHA == fleet pin, csproj refs == manifest edges, global.json == fleet-current, README mandatory sections, tag/Release/NuGet traceability
5. fixture-tested exceptions
6. Record Confirmed, Refuted, or Partial evidence and re-scope dependents without implementing unapproved fixes.
7. Update documentation, migration notes, API/release baselines, and roadmap evidence; run every validation command and attach results.

## Architecture guidance

Keep cross-repository policy and generated inventory in Atya.Roadmap/platform authority; package repositories consume generated artifacts and must not fork policy copies.

## Compatibility and migration

Old drift workflow retired after one overlapping cycle.

## Security and privacy considerations

Apply least privilege, treat repository and payload inputs as hostile, redact secrets and internal diagnostics by default, bound untrusted input size/cardinality, and add negative/adversarial tests for the affected trust boundary.

## Testing strategy

Translate every acceptance criterion into an automated regression, conformance, fixture, or scenario test where possible. Include negative and boundary cases; preserve existing tests. Source-specific validation: Seeded-drift canary..

## Documentation work

Update Atya.Roadmap README/architecture material, migration or release notes, and Atya.Roadmap evidence. Link any ADR and identify the last compatible behavior/version.

## Measurable acceptance criteria

- All findings of both source reviews would have been caught by the check set (walk the list and prove coverage); scheduled run green on the repaired fleet, red on seeded drift.

## Definition of done

- All acceptance criteria pass with durable evid

records.title: Test dependencies and ordering — conditional execution chains
records.body:
## Description

Allow declaring dependencies between tests so that a test is only executed if its prerequisite tests have passed. This avoids running a cascade of integration tests when the setup/environment test has already failed, saving time and producing cleaner reports.

## Current behavior

- Tests are executed in discovery order (alphabetical or as listed).
- No dependency mechanism — all tests run regardless of previous results.
- A failed setup test still triggers all downstream tests, which all fail with confusing errors.

## Expected behavior

- Tests can declare dependencies via `# guitest:` directives:
  ```python
  # guitest: show
  # guitest: depends: test_setup_environment
  def test_integration_scenario():
      ...
  ```
- If a dependency fails, dependent tests are automatically marked as "skipped (dependency failed)".
- Dependency chains are visualized in the GUI (tree or graph view).
- Circular dependencies are detected and reported as configuration errors.
- Independent tests (no dependencies) can still run in any order.

## Implementation ideas

1. Extend `# guitest:` parser to support `depends:` directive.
2. Build a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of test dependencies.
3. Topological sort for execution order.
4. Skip dependents immediately when a prerequisite fails.
5. GUI: show dependency arrows or indent dependent tests under their parent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Tests can declare dependencies on other tests
- [ ] Dependent tests are skipped when prerequisites fail
- [ ] Skipped tests show reason: "dependency X failed"
- [ ] Circular dependencies are detected and reported
- [ ] Execution order respects the dependency graph
- [ ] Independent tests are unaffected

records.title: Rebuild Video.availableLanguages as one cycle-safe, recursively-correct source of truth
records.body:
## Problem Statement

`Video.availableLanguages` is supposed to be the union of a video's own published-variant languages plus every language available anywhere in its published descendant tree (a collection/series/featureFilm can nest videos to arbitrary depth via a self-referential `children` relation). In practice it is maintained by hand-rolled, incremental application code scattered across many mutation call sites, and that code is provably wrong in more than one way:

- Removing a video from a container never re-checks whether the language it provided should disappear from that container — by the time reconciliation fires, the relation is already severed, so the old parent is structurally unreachable and the stale language sticks forever.
- The one cascade that does exist stops after a single hop up the tree, so a three-level-deep container (e.g. `featureFilm` → `series` → `video`) never receives an update at its outermost level even on the already-shipped add path.
- At least two more call sites bypass the shared helper entirely with their own hand-rolled array math and their own, different definition of "parent," and one wired-up worker job overwrites the field from a video's own variants only, silently discarding every child-derived language on any container it touches.
- The underlying `children`/`parents` relation is an unguarded graph (not a tree) with no cycle prevention anywhere — nothing stops a video from being made its own ancestor today.
- None of this is meaningfully tested: the one existing test for the cascade only ever wires up a single level of parents, so it could not have caught the depth bug even though it technically exists; the parent-variant creation/cleanup functions have placeholder tests that assert only `typeof fn === 'function'`.

The user-facing symptom is real: catalog consumers (the public Arclight API, the watch app, journeys-admin) can show a collection as missing a language its own children actually have, or keep showing a language nothing provides anymore. This is the confirmed root cause blocking two in-flight PRs (#9384, #9386) and the umbrella VMT-318 fix (Wonder Series language-sync bug, tracked under issue #9381).

## Solution

Replace the scattered, incremental, hand-mutated maintenance of `availableLanguages` with a single correct calculation, used everywhere the field is ever written, plus a batch verifier that can prove (and self-heal) the invariant across the whole catalog on demand. Concretely:

- One recompute function becomes the only way this field is ever set. It is implemented as an application-level, cycle-safe upward walk (not a raw SQL recursive query) so it stays testable through this repo's existing mocked-Prisma test seam without introducing a new integration-test tier.
- Every mutation, worker, and script that can affect a video's derived language set is routed through this one function, cascading all the way to the root, not stopping at one hop.
- The underlying `children`/`parents` relation gets an explicit cycle guard in the walker itself (defense against data that the application can already create today) and the one worker that maintains that relation from `childIds` gets hardened from an additive-only sync to a true replace, removing a latent drift risk.
- A separate, adjacent correctness bug in a sibling field (`variantLanguages` missing the `published: true` filter that its sibling `variantLanguagesCount` already has) is fixed in the same pass, since it's the same file, the same bug family, and already understood.
- A batch verifier walks the whole catalog bottom-up, diffs computed values against stored ones, and can self-heal drift — turning "we hope every write path is complete" into something provable and re-checkable, independent of whether every future call site remembers to do the right thing.

## User Stories

1. As an engineer maintaining `apis/api-media`, I want exactly one function that computes `availableLanguages`, so that there is no second, disagreeing implementation to drift out of sync with the first.
2. As an engineer, I want that function to walk all the way to the root of a container hierarchy, so that a three-or-more-level-deep collection's outermost container reflects a language change made anywhere below it.
3. As an engineer, I want removing a video from a container's children to trigger the same recompute as adding one, so that a language provided only by the removed child disappears from the old parent instead of sticking around forever.
4. As an engineer, I want the recompute to work by full recalculation from current source data (own published variants ∪ each live child's current value) rather than incremental add/remove array mutation, so that the result is self-correcting by construction instead of accumulating drift from a missed edge case.

records.title: EPIC: Incubate the Neo4j Operations skill and adapter
records.body:
## Objective

Incubate a reusable, safe, consistent, and auditable Neo4j operations skill and shared Python adapter; prove domain-neutral reuse; then make an evidence-based stop/continue decision.

## Boundaries

- Only this repository may be modified.
- Evidence and consumer repositories remain read-only.
- The skill guides governed workflows; the adapter owns shared operational behavior; the official driver owns connectivity; consumers own schemas and business rules.
- No implementation begins until the user approves a specific issue, group, or cycle after Phase 1.
- Draft PR #1 adds the durable root repository instructions and should merge before product implementation.

## Architectural decisions

- [ ] #3 — Packaging, versioning, and supported Python/driver/server/Cypher matrix
- [ ] #4 — Stable adapter interface
- [ ] #7 — APOC and GDS dependency policy
- [ ] #8 — Trusted Cypher templates and dynamic identifiers
- [ ] #9 — Cycle 1 destructive-operation prohibition/denial policy and any justified later authorization model
- [ ] #5 — Load-run and checkpoint lifecycle, required for Cycle 2
- [ ] #6 — Operational metadata storage boundary, required for Cycle 2

Cycle 1 requires #3, #4, #7, #8, and a complete #9 decision that defaults destructive execution to prohibited/deferred. Cycle 2 requires #5 and #6. Dependent implementation must not begin until its linked decisions are accepted.

## Cycle 1 — Safe operational core and first reuse proof

Outcome: an installable, secret-safe, bounded read/execute foundation proven against disposable Neo4j and the visualizer provider contract.

- [ ] #10 — Python package and repository quality foundation
- [ ] #27 — Foundational operation result and error contract
- [ ] #12 — Validated secret-safe configuration
- [ ] #13 — Driver lifecycle, diagnostics, and access modes
- [ ] #14 — Named parameterized execution
- [ ] #15 — Transaction, retry, and timeout policy
- [ ] #21 — Core disposable Neo4j integration infrastructure
- [ ] #16 — Operation-specific reporting enrichment and reconciliation
- [ ] #17 — Read-only schema and plan inspection
- [ ] #22 — Legacy evidence and disposition register
- [ ] #23 — Visualizer read-only provider contract
- [ ] #11 — Installable Neo4j operations skill, completed after the Cycle 1 runtime

### Cycle 1 exit criteria

- Package and skill install/discover in clean supported environments.
- Diagnostics select the database explicitly and remain read-only.
- Named operations enforce parameters, query trust, access mode, bounds, retries, timeouts, and redaction.
- Disposable integration tests verify lifecycle, rollback, failure, and cleanup across the approved matrix.
- The visualizer fixture uses the stable provider interface without consumer or domain code entering the core.
- No unresolved decision blocks the delivered surface.

## Cycle 2 — Recoverable loading and independent reuse validation

Outcome: domain-neutral run/checkpoint and idempotent loading behavior proven by two independent write scenarios, followed by an incubation decision.

- [ ] #18 — Guarded destructive workflows, only if #9 permits them
- [ ] #19 — Domain-neutral load-run/checkpoint persistence
- [ ] #20 — Idempotent neutral entity/relationship loading
- [ ] #24 — Market-intelligence provider contract
- [ ] #25 — Second neutral write reuse case
- [ ] #26 — Incubation stop/continue review

### Cycle 2 exit criteria

- Run/checkpoint transitions, storage, concurrency, resume, and recovery follow accepted decisions.
- Repeated neutral entity/relationship loads do not duplicate data and reconcile structured counters.
- Market-intelligence and the independent content-engine-derived fixture use the same public adapter without domain-specific additions.
- Any destructive capability is denied by default and satisfies authorization, preview, bounds, recovery, and audit controls.
- #26 records inventory disposition, compatibility evidence, residual risks, external consumer dependencies, and a stop/continue recommendation.

## Readiness and gates

Ready for Cycle 1 decision work now: #3, #4, #7, #8, and #9. Decisions #5 and #6 may wait for Cycle 2.

Ready after explicit Phase 2 authorization and applicable decisions: #10 and the disposition-register work in #22. Issue #27 follows #4 and #10.

Ready only after the Cycle 1 runtime foundation: #11.

Blocked by their recorded decisions or foundations: #12–#21 and #23–#26. Optional extension variants in #21 depend on #7, but the core harness does not.

Consumer-side adoption is never included. Required changes in visualizer, market-intelligence, content-engine, or another consumer remain external dependencies requiring separate repository-specific authorization.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every child issue has scope, exclusions, dependencies, controls, acceptance criteria, tests, evidence, reporting, and unresolved questions.
- [ ] Required ADRs precede dependent implementation.
- [ ] Safety verification covers secrets, databas
